chunks: "The main ones are ferrite, powdered iron and its relatives, silicon steel, and amorphous or nanocrystalline alloys, and air for RF.
Ferrite is a ceramic of iron oxide with manganese-zinc or nickel-zinc.
It has high permeability, low eddy-current loss because it's an insulator, so it's the standard for transformers and inductors from tens of kilohertz up to a few megahertz.
The catch is a relatively low saturation, around 0. 3 to 0. 5 tesla, and it saturates hard, so for DC-biased inductors it's gapped.
Nickel-zinc has lower permeability but works to hundreds of megahertz, so it's used for EMI beads.
Powdered iron and its cousins, sendust, high-flux and MPP, are made of metal particles in an insulating binder.
That gives a distributed air gap, so low permeability, maybe 10 to 200, saturation around 1 tesla or more, and soft saturation where the inductance falls gradually.
That's why they're used in buck converter inductors and DC chokes. Laminated silicon steel has the highest saturation, around 1.
5 to 2 tesla, but eddy currents limit it to line frequencies, so it's for 50 or 60 hertz transformers.
Nanocrystalline and amorphous ribbon have very high permeability and good saturation, around 1.
2 tesla, with low loss, so they're used in common-mode chokes and high-power medium-frequency transformers. I pick based on frequency, DC bias, losses, and cost."
